hmmt-feb-2022-guts-01.title: Approximate by the circumcircle
hmmt-feb-2022-guts-01.body:
A regular $n$-gon with $n$ large is almost its circumcircle: its perimeter is $2nR\sin\frac\pi n\approx2\pi R$ and its area is $\frac n2R^2\sin\frac{2\pi}n\approx\pi R^2$. Since the perimeter is $6.28\approx2\pi$, the circumradius is $R\approx1$ (more precisely $R\approx0.9995$), so the area is $\approx\pi R^2\approx3.14$, which rounds to $3$.

**Answer: 3**

hmmt-feb-2022-guts-02.title: Count the acute triangles
hmmt-feb-2022-guts-02.body:
There are $\binom53=10$ triangles. A triangle inscribed in the circumcircle is acute iff it contains the center, i.e. iff each of its three arcs is less than a semicircle. Among the triangles of a regular pentagon, the three vertices either are consecutive (arcs $72^\circ,72^\circ,216^\circ$: obtuse) or consist of two adjacent vertices and the vertex opposite their side (arcs $72^\circ,144^\circ,144^\circ$: acute). There are $5$ of the latter. So $p=\frac5{10}=\frac12$ and $10p=5$.

**Answer: 5**

hmmt-feb-2022-guts-03.title: One prime, five ones
hmmt-feb-2022-guts-03.body:
The product is prime iff exactly one die shows a prime ($2$, $3$ or $5$) and all other five dice show $1$. There are $6$ choices for the die showing the prime and $3$ choices of the prime, so the probability is $\frac{6\cdot3}{6^6}=\frac{18}{46656}=\frac1{2592}$. Hence $100a+b=100+2592=2692$.

**Answer: 2692**

hmmt-feb-2022-guts-04.title: Fractional parts
hmmt-feb-2022-guts-04.body:
Since $[b]$ is an integer, $\langle a\rangle$ has tenths digit $6$ and fractional part $0.6$ after rounding; so $a=i+\alpha$ with $i$ an integer and $\alpha\in[0.55,0.65)$. Since $[a]$ is an integer, $\langle b\rangle$ has fractional part $0.3$, so $b=j+\beta$ with $\beta\in[0.25,0.35)$.

Then $\langle a\rangle=i+0.6$, $[a]=i+1$ (as $\alpha\ge0.5$), $[b]=j$ (as $\beta<0.5$), $\langle b\rangle=j+0.3$. The two equations both read $i+j=98$. So $a+b=98+\alpha+\beta\ge98+0.55+0.25=98.8$, with equality attainable (e.g. $a=49.55$, $b=49.25$). Hence the minimum of $[10(a+b)]$ is $[988]=988$.

**Answer: 988**

hmmt-feb-2022-guts-05.title: Blocks of powers of two
hmmt-feb-2022-guts-05.body:
Write $X_k$ for $2^k$ padded with leading zeros to four digits, so the big number is the concatenation $N=X_0X_1\cdots X_{13}$ (the leading zeros of $X_0=0001$ are dropped) and the divisor is $D=X_0X_1\cdots X_5$. Because $2^{11}<10^4$, multiplying each block by $2^6$ causes no carries, so $2^6\cdot X_0\cdots X_5=X_6X_7\cdots X_{11}$. Therefore
$$X_0\cdots X_{11}=D\cdot10^{24}+X_6\cdots X_{11}=D\,(10^{24}+64),$$
so $D\mid X_0\cdots X_{11}$, and $N=X_0\cdots X_{11}\cdot10^8+X_{12}X_{13}\equiv X_{12}X_{13}\pmod D$. Since $X_{12}X_{13}=40968192<D$, the remainder is $40968192$.

**Answer: 40968192**

hmmt-feb-2022-guts-06.title: Two orientations of each polygon
hmmt-feb-2022-guts-06.body:
$ICAO$ is a square, $VENTI$ a regular pentagon, $ALBEDO$ a regular hexagon; they share the vertices $A,O$ (square and hexagon, a common side), $E$ (pentagon and hexagon) and $I$ (square and pentagon).

Fix the hexagon $ALBEDO$. The square $ICAO$ on the side $AO$ has two possible orientations (on either side of $AO$). In the hexagon, the diagonal $OE$ makes angle $\angle AOE=90^\circ$ with the side $OA$, so in both orientations $I$ lies on line $EO$: on ray $OE$ inside the hexagon, or on the opposite side of $O$.

In the pentagon $VENTI$, $E$ and $I$ are two apart (a diagonal), as are $I$ and $N$, so $IE=IN$ (both diagonals) and $\angle EIN=36^\circ$. For a given position of $I$ and $E$ the two orientations of the pentagon put $N$ at mirror positions across line $EI$. Since $O$ lies on line $EI$, $ON$ is the same for both pentagon orientations. So $ON$ depends only on the orientation of the square.

With $IN=IE=1$: if $I$ is between $O$ and $E$ then $OI=a$ with $a(\sqrt3-1)=1$ (hexagon side $a$, $OE=a\sqrt3$) and $\angle OIN=144^\circ$; if $O$ is between $I$ and $E$ then $a(\sqrt3+1)=1$ and $\angle OIN=36^\circ$. These give different values of $ON$ (computed by the law of cosines: $ON^2=OI^2+1-2\,OI\cos\angle OIN$), so there are exactly $2$ possible values.

**Answer: 2**

hmmt-feb-2022-guts-07.title: Only the end of the process matters
hmmt-feb-2022-guts-07.body:
Since there are only $2$ blue balls, blue can exceed red only when at most $3$ balls remain: with one ball left (it is blue), or with $3$ balls left being $2$ blue and $1$ red (two balls left being one of each is a tie). So the condition holds iff the last ball removed is blue (probability $\frac15$), or the last ball is red and the two blue balls are the second-to-last and third-to-last removed (probability $\frac1{\binom{10}2}=\frac1{45}$). These cases are disjoint, so the probability is $\frac15+\frac1{45}=\frac{10}{45}=\frac29$, and $100a+b=209$.

**Answer: 209**

hmmt-feb-2022-guts-08.title: Exponent equation
hmmt-feb-2022-guts-08.body:
Let $n=p_1^{e_1}\cdots p_k^{e_k}$. Then $\frac{\tau(n^2)}{\tau(n)}=\prod_{i=1}^k\frac{2e_i+1}{e_i+1}=3$. Each factor is at least $\frac32$ (for $e\ge1$) and $\left(\frac32\right)^3>3$, so $k\le2$. For $k=1$: $2e+1=3(e+1)$ gives $e=-2$, impossible. For $k=2$: $(2e_1+1)(2e_2+1)=3(e_1+1)(e_2+1)$ simplifies to $(e_1-1)(e_2-1)=3$, so $\{e_1,e_2\}=\{2,4\}$. Then $\frac{\tau(n^7)}{\tau(n)}=\frac{(14+1)(28+1)}{3\cdot5}=29$.

**Answer: 29**

hmmt-feb-2022-guts-09.title: Count intersections of pieces
hmmt-feb-2022-guts-09.body:
Call a *C-shape* an $E$-shape without its middle ray; so an $E$-shape is a ray together with a C-shape. Two C-shapes (each made of a segment and two rays) can meet in at most $6$ points, a C-shape and a ray in at most $2$, and two rays in at most $1$. Writing $E_1=r_1\cup C_1$ and $E_2=r_2\cup C_2$,
$$N\le|C_1\cap C_2|+|C_1\cap r_2|+|r_1\cap C_2|+|r_1\cap r_2|\le6+2+2+1=11.$$
This is attained: a random search over pairs of $E$-shapes finds configurations with exactly $11$ intersection points and none with more.

**Answer: 11**

hmmt-feb-2022-guts-10.title: Shape of $n$ and casework
hmmt-feb-2022-guts-10.body:
A number with exactly six divisors is $p^5$ or $p^2q$ ($p,q$ distinct primes). For $p^5$ the divisors $1,p,p^2,\dots$ need $p\ge2$, which holds for all $p$, but then $p^5<100$ forces $p=2$: $n=32$ with divisors $1,2,4,8,16,32$ (each at least double the previous): loose.

For $n=p^2q<100$ we need $p\le7$. The divisors are $1,p,p^2,q,pq,p^2q$.
- $p=2$: divisors $1,2,4,q,2q,4q$. For $q=3$ we get $3<2\cdot2$; for $q=5,7$ we get $q<2\cdot4$; so $q\ge11$, and for such $q$ all gaps are fine. With $n=4q<100$: $q=11,13,17,19,23$, giving $n=44,52,68,76,92$.
- $p=3$: divisors $1,3,9,q,3q,9q$; $q$ must avoid $[2,5]$ and $[5,17]$, so $q\ge19$, but then $9q>100$: none.
- $p=5$: $n=25q<100$ gives $q\in\{2,3\}$; $q=2$: divisors $1,2,5,10,25,50$ ok ($n=50$); $q=3$: $1,3,5,\dots$ has $5<2\cdot3$: no.
- $p=7$: $n=49q<100$ gives $q=2$: divisors $1,2,7,14,49,98$: ok ($n=98$).

The loose numbers are $32,44,50,52,68,76,92,98$, with sum $512$.

**Answer: 512**

hmmt-feb-2022-guts-11.title: Sector minus an equilateral triangle
hmmt-feb-2022-guts-11.body:
The sector $OP_2P_4$ has central angle $60^\circ$, so area $\frac\pi6$. The region is this sector minus triangle $OXY$. The chord $P_1P_5$ subtends $120^\circ$, so its distance from $O$ is $\cos60^\circ=\frac12$, and it is perpendicular to the bisector $OP_3$. Triangle $OXY$ has apex angle $60^\circ$ (between $OP_2$ and $OP_4$) and altitude $\frac12$, so it is equilateral with side $\frac{1}{\sqrt3}$ and area $\frac{\sqrt3}{12}$. Hence $A=\frac\pi6-\frac{\sqrt3}{12}$ and $120A=20\pi-10\sqrt3\approx62.83-17.32=45.5$, so $\lfloor120A\rfloor=45$.

**Answer: 45**

hmmt-feb-2022-guts-12.title: Intersection of four disks
hmmt-feb-2022-guts-12.body:
The property says: every point $P$ with all four angles $\angle APB,\dots,\angle DPA$ greater than $60^\circ$ lies in the interior of $\Gamma$. Let $X_1,\dots,X_4$ be the apexes of the equilateral triangles $ABX_1$, $BCX_2$, $CDX_3$, $DAX_4$ erected inward, and $\Omega_i$ their circumcircles. The set of points $P$ with all four angles above $60^\circ$ is the intersection of the four open disks bounded by the $\Omega_i$, and $\Gamma$ must contain it; we need the smallest circle containing this intersection.

Let $\Omega_1\cap\Omega_2=\{B,B'\}$ and define $C',D',A'$ similarly. The intersection region has vertices $A',B',C',D'$ (a square by symmetry) and the minimal enclosing circle is the circumcircle of $A'B'C'D'$. We have $\angle AB'D'=\angle AB'D=60^\circ$ and $\angle AD'B'=60^\circ$, so $\triangle AB'D'$ is equilateral; its height is the distance from $A$ to the diagonal line $B'D'$ through the center of the square, namely $\frac1{\sqrt2}$, so its side is $\frac{\sqrt6}3$. This is the diameter of the circle. Its area is $\pi\cdot\frac14\cdot\frac69=\frac\pi6$ (numerically the farthest point of the region from the center is at distance $\frac1{\sqrt6}$), so $100a+b=106$.

**Answer: 106**

hmmt-feb-2022-guts-13.title: Palindromic substitution
hmmt-feb-2022-guts-13.body:
$x=0$ is not a root, so divide by $x^2$: $\left(x^2+\frac1{x^2}\right)+3\left(x+\frac1x\right)+3=0$, i.e. with $y=x+\frac1x$: $y^2+3y+1=0$, so $y=\frac{-3\pm\sqrt5}2$.

For $y=\frac{-3+\sqrt5}2\approx-0.38$, $|y|<2$ so $x+\frac1x=y$ has two non-real roots of modulus $1$ (their product is $1$ and they are conjugates). For $y=\frac{-3-\sqrt5}2<-2$, the two roots are negative reals that are reciprocals of each other, so the sum of their absolute values is $|y|=\frac{3+\sqrt5}2$. Total: $1+1+\frac{3+\sqrt5}2=\frac{7+\sqrt5}2$. So $a=7,b=1,c=5,d=2$ and $1000a+100b+10c+d=7152$.

**Answer: 7152**

hmmt-feb-2022-guts-14.title: Inscribed rectangle $s\times s\sqrt3$
hmmt-feb-2022-guts-14.body:
Following the official solution, the largest regular hexagon that fits is governed by the $s\times s\sqrt3$ rectangle spanned by four of its vertices: the hexagon of side $s$ fits in the $20\times22$ rectangle $ABCD$ ($AB=20$, $BC=22$) exactly when a tilted $s\times s\sqrt3$ rectangle fits. Let $XYZW$ be an inscribed such rectangle with $X\in AB$, $Y\in BC$, $XY=s$, $YZ=s\sqrt3$, and put $BX=a$, $BY=b$. By similar triangles $AX=b\sqrt3$ and $CY=a\sqrt3$. So
$$a+b\sqrt3=20,\qquad a\sqrt3+b=22,$$
giving $a=11\sqrt3-10$, $b=10\sqrt3-11$ and $s^2=a^2+b^2=884-440\sqrt3$. The hexagon's area is $\frac{3\sqrt3}2s^2=\frac{3\sqrt3}{2}(884-440\sqrt3)=1326\sqrt3-1980$. So $100a+10b+c=132600+30+1980=134610$.

**Answer: 134610**

hmmt-feb-2022-guts-15.title: Count ordered triples, then unordered
hmmt-feb-2022-guts-15.body:
Let $n=2020$ and write $a=2^{p_1}3^{q_1}$, $b=2^{p_2}3^{q_2}$, $c=2^{p_3}3^{q_3}$ with $p_1+p_2+p_3=q_1+q_2+q_3=n$. The condition $\gcd=1$ means at least one $p_i=0$ and at least one $q_i=0$. The number of nonnegative solutions with $p_1+p_2+p_3=n$ and some $p_i=0$ is $\binom{n+2}2-\binom{n-1}2=3n$, and the same for the $q_i$. So there are $9n^2$ ordered triples.

Let $\ell$ be the number of unordered triples with distinct entries and $m$ the number with exactly two equal entries (all three equal is impossible since then $a=b=c>1$ has $\gcd>1$). Then $9n^2=6\ell+3m$. For two equal entries $a=b$: for the prime $2$ either $c$ takes $2^n$ (and $a=b$ has none) or $a=b$ each take $2^{n/2}$ (and $c$ has none) -- $2$ ways, and similarly $2$ ways for the prime $3$: $m=4$. The number of triples with $a\le b\le c$ is $N=\ell+m=\frac{9n^2-3m}6+m=\frac{9\cdot2020^2+6}{6}=\frac{9\cdot2020^2-12}{6}+4=6120602$. So $N\equiv602\pmod{1000}$.

**Answer: 602**

hmmt-feb-2022-guts-16.title: Power of the point $D$
hmmt-feb-2022-guts-16.body:
Let $AD=DE=EF=x$, $a=BC$, $b=CA$, $c=AB$, $s$ the semiperimeter, and assume $AB<AC$ (then $\sin B=\frac{AD}{AB}$ is larger than in the mirror-image labelling). Let $\Gamma$ touch $BC$ at $T$. The excircle lies beyond $BC$, so the points on the line from $A$ are, in order, $A,D,E,F$ at distances $0,x,2x,3x$ from $A$. By power of the point $D$, $DT^2=DE\cdot DF=x\cdot2x$, so $DT=x\sqrt2$. The tangent length from $A$ to $\Gamma$ is $s$, so $s^2=AE\cdot AF=2x\cdot3x=6x^2$, i.e. $s=x\sqrt6$.

Since $CT=s-b$ and $BC=BD+DT+TC$, we get $BD=a-x\sqrt2-(x\sqrt6-b)=a+b-x(\sqrt2+\sqrt6)$. With $a+b=2s-c=2x\sqrt6-c$, $BD=x(\sqrt6-\sqrt2)-c$. In the right triangle $ABD$: $c^2=x^2+\bigl[x(\sqrt6-\sqrt2)-c\bigr]^2$, which simplifies to $x^2(9-4\sqrt3)=xc\,(2\sqrt6-2\sqrt2)$. Hence
$$\sin B=\frac xc=\frac{2\sqrt6-2\sqrt2}{9-4\sqrt3}=\frac{6\sqrt2+10\sqrt6}{33}=\frac{\sqrt{72}+\sqrt{600}}{33}.$$
Since $\sqrt2$ and $\sqrt6$ are linearly independent over $\mathbb Q$, any expression $\frac{\sqrt a+\sqrt b}c$ equal to this has $a=\frac{72c^2}{33^2}$, $b=\frac{600c^2}{33^2}$ (or swapped), which are integers only for $33\mid c$; the minimum is $c=33$, giving $a+b+c=72+600+33=705$.

**Answer: 705**

hmmt-feb-2022-guts-17.title: Piecewise monotone on each dyadic interval
hmmt-feb-2022-guts-17.body:
Let $f(x)=3\cdot2^{\lfloor\log_2x\rfloor}-x$. For $x\in[2^i,2^{i+1})$, $f(x)=3\cdot2^i-x$, a line segment from $(2^i,2^{i+1})$ down to (but not including) $(2^{i+1},2^i)$. So $f>0$ there and the equation is equivalent to $\frac{f(x)^{16}}{x^{13}}=2022$. On $[2^i,2^{i+1})$ the function $\frac{(3\cdot2^i-x)^{16}}{x^{13}}$ is strictly decreasing, from $\frac{(2^{i+1})^{16}}{2^{13i}}=2^{3i+16}$ at $x=2^i$ to (limit) $\frac{(2^i)^{16}}{2^{13(i+1)}}=2^{3i-13}$ at $x=2^{i+1}$ (not attained). It takes the value $2022$ exactly once iff $2^{3i-13}<2022\le2^{3i+16}$; since $2^{10}<2022<2^{11}$ this is $-1\le i\le7$ (for $i=7$: $2^{8}<2022\le2^{37}$; for $i=8$: $2^{11}>2022$ so fails; for $i=-2$: $2^{10}<2022$ and $2^{-6+16}=2^{10}<2022$ fails). That gives $i=-1,0,\dots,7$: $9$ solutions.

**Answer: 9**

hmmt-feb-2022-guts-18.title: Graph automorphisms
hmmt-feb-2022-guts-18.body:
Since $\pi$ maps the finite set of pairs $\{m,n\}$ with prime sum into itself injectively, it permutes this set, so $m+n$ composite implies $\pi(m)+\pi(n)$ composite. Taking $m=n=1$: $2$ is prime, so $2\pi(1)$ is prime, forcing $\pi(1)=1$.

*Parity.* For $k=2,4,6,10$, $1+k$ is prime, so $1+\pi(k)$ is prime. An odd $\pi(k)\ge3$ would make $1+\pi(k)$ an even number $\ge4$, and $\pi(k)=8$ gives the composite $9$; so $\pi(k)\in\{2,4,6,10\}$ and $\pi$ permutes $\{2,4,6,10\}$. Then $\pi$ permutes $\{3,5,7,8,9\}$. Since $8+3,8+5,8+9$ are prime, $\pi(8)+\pi(3),\pi(8)+\pi(5),\pi(8)+\pi(9)$ are prime; if $\pi(8)$ were odd these three sums would force $\pi(3),\pi(5),\pi(9)$ all to be even, but $8$ is the only even number available. So $\pi(8)=8$, and $\pi$ permutes the odd numbers $\{3,5,7,9\}$ and the even numbers $\{2,4,6,10\}$.

*Structure.* Among these, the pairs (odd, even) with composite sum are $3+6=9$, $9+6=15$, $5+4=9$, $5+10=15$, $7+2=9$; all other odd--even sums are prime. $\pi$ must preserve this graph, which consists of the path $3-6-9$ (middle vertex even), the path $4-5-10$ (middle vertex odd) and the edge $7-2$. Since $\pi$ preserves parity, it fixes each component: the middle vertices $6$ and $5$ are fixed, hence also $7$ and $2$, while the ends can be swapped independently: $3\leftrightarrow9$ and $4\leftrightarrow10$. This gives $2\cdot2=4$ permutations, and each indeed works.

**Answer: 4**

hmmt-feb-2022-guts-19.title: Power of a point and a radical axis
hmmt-feb-2022-guts-19.body:
The right angle is at $B$. From $BD\perp AC$: $AD\cdot AC=AB^2$. The power of $A$ with respect to $\omega$ is $AD\cdot AC=AB^2$, so the tangent from $A$ to $\omega$ along line $AB$ has length $AB$; the tangency point other than $B$ is $B'$, the reflection of $B$ over $A$, and $BB'=2AB=4$.

Let $Y$ be the second intersection of $\omega$ with line $BC$. Power of $B$: $BY\cdot BC=BB'^2=16$, so $BY=\frac{16}5$.

Line $AX$ is perpendicular to $BO$, and $A$ has power $AB^2$ with respect to $\omega$ and also $AB^2$ with respect to the degenerate circle at $B$; so $AX$ is the radical axis of $\omega$ and the point-circle $B$. Hence $X$ satisfies $XB^2=XY\cdot XC$. With $BX=t$: $t^2=(t-\frac{16}5)(t-5)=t^2-\frac{41}5t+16$, so $t=\frac{80}{41}$. Therefore $100a+b=8000+41=8041$.

**Answer: 8041**

hmmt-feb-2022-guts-20.title: Cycle lengths of $20$ and $21$
hmmt-feb-2022-guts-20.body:
The conditions say the cycle length $a$ of $20$ divides $20$ and the cycle length $b$ of $21$ divides $21$. They cannot lie in the same cycle: then $a=b$ would divide $\gcd(20,21)=1$, so $a=b=1$, but then $20$ and $21$ would not be in one cycle. So they are in different cycles of lengths $a\mid20$ and $b\mid21$.

For fixed $a,b$ with $a+b\le100$, the number of permutations in which $20$ lies in a cycle of length $a$ and $21$ in a cycle of length $b$ (different cycles) is: choose the other $a-1$ elements of $20$'s cycle and $b-1$ of $21$'s cycle, arrange them in cycles in $(a-1)!$ and $(b-1)!$ ways, and permute the rest in $(100-a-b)!$ ways, totalling $\frac{98!}{(a-1)!(b-1)!(100-a-b)!}(a-1)!(b-1)!(100-a-b)!=98!$. So each pair $(a,b)$ has probability $\frac{98!}{100!}=\frac1{9900}$. There are $6$ divisors of $20$ and $4$ divisors of $21$, so the probability is $\frac{6\cdot4}{9900}=\frac2{825}$, and $100a+b=200+825=1025$.

**Answer: 1025**

hmmt-feb-2022-guts-21.title: Pick's theorem on two lattices
hmmt-feb-2022-guts-21.body:
Call a point *central* if it has the form $(x+\frac12,y+\frac12)$. Let $K$ be the area of $ABC$ ($K=31500$), $I_1,B_1$ the numbers of interior and boundary lattice points, $I_c,B_c$ the numbers of interior and boundary central points.

Rotate by $45^\circ$ and scale by $\sqrt2$: lattice points and central points together become a lattice (the original lattice together with the central points), and the triangle has area $2K$. With $I_2,B_2$ the numbers of interior and boundary points of this combined lattice, $I_2=I_1+I_c$ and $B_2=B_1+B_c$. Pick's theorem on both lattices gives $K=I_1+\frac{B_1}2-1$ and $2K=I_2+\frac{B_2}2-1$. Subtracting, $K=(I_2-I_1)+\frac{B_2-B_1}2=I_c+\frac{B_c}2$, so
$$I_c=K-\frac{B_c}2.$$
The area is $K=\frac12\lvert200\cdot330-100\cdot30\rvert=31500$. The numbers of central points on $AB$, $BC$, $CA$ are $0$, $10$, $30$ respectively (they occur where the segment passes through half-integer points: $AB$ has direction $(2,1)$ and contains none; $BC$ has direction $(-170,230)=10(-17,23)$ and $CA$ has direction $(-30,-330)=30(-1,-11)$), so $B_c=40$ and $I_c=31500-20=31480$. (A direct count over all $(x,y)$ confirms this.)

**Answer: 31480**

hmmt-feb-2022-guts-22.title: Match values, then use congruences
hmmt-feb-2022-guts-22.body:
*Matching.* $a\ge0$ is forced by the answer being nonnegative, and the largest value $4.39\cdot10^{12}$ must be at an endpoint of the range of inputs, i.e. $f(177\,883)$ or $f(858\,522)$. Since $858\,522$ is close to $796\,921$, their values would be close, so the largest value is $f(177\,883)$. Reducing mod $2$ pins $f(796\,921)\approx1.32\cdot10^{12}$, and mod $5$ (using that $f(1)\equiv f(3)\equiv0$ so $f(x)\equiv a(x-1)(x-3)$) gives $a\equiv3\pmod5$ and $f(348\,710)\approx1.78\cdot10^{12}$, $f(858\,522)\approx1.98\cdot10^{12}$.

*Finishing.* Mod $9$ the finite differences give $a\equiv5\pmod9$, so $a\equiv23\pmod{45}$, and $a\ge68$ is ruled out by size (e.g. the slope $f'$ is between $f'(260000)\approx-1.5\cdot10^6$ and $f'(830000)\approx10^6$, so $2a$ is just under $50$). Hence $a=23$.

*Check.* The polynomial $f(x)=23x^2-27\,370\,172x+8\,529\,708\,870\,514$ indeed takes the four given values at the four given inputs.

**Answer: 23**

hmmt-feb-2022-guts-23.title: A rectangle from translates
hmmt-feb-2022-guts-23.body:
The trapezoid has height $\sqrt{25^2-7^2}=24$ (the horizontal offset of each leg is $\frac{31-17}2=7$). Let $M$ be the midpoint of $PQ$; since $AP=CQ$, $M$ lies on the midline of the trapezoid (the segment halfway between $AB$ and $CD$).

Let $B'C'$ be the translate of $BC$ (by a vector parallel to $AB$) with midpoint $M$. Then $MB'=MC'=\frac{25}2=MP=MQ$, so $B'$ and $C'$ lie on the circle with diameter $PQ$, and on the lines $AB$ and $CD$ respectively (as $B'C'$ is a translate of the leg $BC$ whose endpoints are on those lines and $M$ is on the midline). Define $A',D'$ similarly from $DA$. These four points are the four intersection points, and $B'D'C'A'$ is a rectangle whose height is the height of the trapezoid, $24$, and whose width is $\frac12(31-17)=7$. Its area is $24\cdot7=168$.

**Answer: 168**

hmmt-feb-2022-guts-24.title: Recursion for the expected $x$-distance
hmmt-feb-2022-guts-24.body:
By symmetry $a_n=2g(n)$ where $g(n)$ is the expected $|x-x'|$. $S_n$ has side $3^n$. Split it into three vertical strips of width $3^{n-1}$ (meta-columns); the random point lies in the left, middle, right strip with probabilities $\frac38,\frac28,\frac38$ (the middle strip has $2$ of the $8$ copies, the outer ones $3$ each).

- Neighboring strips (probability $2\cdot\frac38\cdot\frac28+2\cdot\frac28\cdot\frac38=\frac38$): by symmetry the expected $x$-distance is the distance between strip centers, $3^{n-1}$.
- Opposite strips (probability $2\cdot\frac38\cdot\frac38=\frac9{32}$): expected distance $2\cdot3^{n-1}$.
- Same strip (probability $\frac{9+4+9}{64}=\frac{11}{32}$): the expected distance is $g(n-1)$.

So $g(n)=3^{n-1}\left(\frac38+2\cdot\frac9{32}\right)+\frac{11}{32}g(n-1)=\frac{15}{16}3^{n-1}+\frac{11}{32}g(n-1)$. Writing $g(n)\sim C\,3^n$: $C=\frac{15}{16\cdot3}+\frac{11}{96}C$, so $C\cdot\frac{85}{96}=\frac5{16}$, $C=\frac6{17}$. Therefore $\lim\frac{a_n}{3^n}=2C=\frac{12}{17}$ and $100a+b=1217$.

**Answer: 1217**

hmmt-feb-2022-guts-25.title: Euler line
hmmt-feb-2022-guts-25.body:
Let $H$ be the orthocenter; $O,G,H$ are collinear with $HG=2OG$. Put $OG=x$. From $\sin A=\frac{BC}{2R}=\frac{15}{18}=\frac56$ we get $\cos A=\frac{\sqrt{11}}6$ and $AH=2R\cos A=3\sqrt{11}$, so $AH^2=99$.

The right angle cannot be at $A$ (then $AG$ would be tangent to the circumcircle at $A$, but $G$ is inside).

*Right angle at $G$ ($AG\perp OG$):* $AO^2=x^2+AG^2$ gives $81=x^2+AG^2$, and since $H,G,O$ are collinear, $AH^2=HG^2+AG^2=4x^2+AG^2=99$. Subtracting: $3x^2=18$, $x=\sqrt6$, $AG=\sqrt{75}=5\sqrt3$; the area is $\frac12\cdot\sqrt6\cdot5\sqrt3=\frac{15\sqrt2}2$.

*Right angle at $O$ ($AO\perp OG$):* then $AH^2=AO^2+OH^2=81+9x^2=99$, so $x=\sqrt2$ and the area is $\frac12\cdot9\cdot\sqrt2=\frac{9\sqrt2}2$.

So $S=\frac{15\sqrt2}2+\frac{9\sqrt2}2=12\sqrt2$ and $S^2=288$.

**Answer: 288**

hmmt-feb-2022-guts-26.title: Branching process and an integral equation
hmmt-feb-2022-guts-26.body:
Each turn uses exactly one draw of one card. For a card of value $x$, its fate is independent of all other cards: each time it is drawn, the computer's number $c$ is uniform on $[0,1]$; with probability $1-x$ the card is lost, and with probability $x$ it is kept and a new card with value $c$ (uniform on $[0,x]$) is added. The total number of turns is the total number of draws, so by linearity the expected number of turns equals the expected total number of draws made by a card and its descendants. Let $f(x)$ be this expectation for a card of value $x$. Then
$$f(x)=1+x\,f(x)+\int_0^xf(t)\,dt.$$
Differentiating: $f'=f+xf'+f$, so $\frac{f'}{f}=\frac2{1-x}$ and $f(x)=\frac C{(1-x)^2}$. At $x=0$ the equation gives $f(0)=1$, so $C=1$ and $f(x)=(1-x)^{-2}$ (one checks it satisfies the integral equation). Hence $E[k]=f(0.9)=\frac1{0.1^2}=100$.

**Answer: 100**

hmmt-feb-2022-guts-27.title: Probability that a point lies in all slabs
hmmt-feb-2022-guts-27.body:
Fix a point $P$ at distance $r$ from the origin. A random rotation of $S$ contains $P$ iff the projection of $P$ onto a uniformly random axis has absolute value at most $1$. The projection of a point at distance $r$ onto a random direction is uniform on $[-r,r]$ (Archimedes), so the probability is $1$ if $r\le1$ and $\frac1r$ if $r>1$. By independence, the probability that $P$ is in all $2022$ rotated slabs is $1$ for $r\le1$ and $r^{-2022}$ for $r>1$. Integrating over space:
$$E[V]=\frac{4\pi}3+4\pi\int_1^\infty r^2\cdot r^{-2022}\,dr=\frac{4\pi}3+\frac{4\pi}{2019}=4\pi\cdot\frac{673+1}{2019}=\frac{2696\pi}{2019}.$$
Since $2696=2^3\cdot337$ and $2019=3\cdot673$ are coprime, $100a+b=269600+2019=271619$.

**Answer: 271619**

hmmt-feb-2022-guts-28.title: Telescoping with the triple-angle formula
hmmt-feb-2022-guts-28.body:
From $\sin3x=3\sin x-4\sin^3x$ we get $\sin^3x=\frac14(3\sin x-\sin3x)$. Taking $x=\frac\pi{3^n}$,
$$3^n\sin^3\frac\pi{3^n}=\frac{3^n}4\left(3\sin\frac\pi{3^n}-\sin\frac\pi{3^{n-1}}\right)=\frac{3\pi}4\left(\frac{\sin(\pi/3^n)}{\pi/3^n}-\frac{\sin(\pi/3^{n-1})}{\pi/3^{n-1}}\right).$$
Summing from $n=1$ to $N$ telescopes to $\frac{3\pi}4\left(\frac{\sin(\pi/3^N)}{\pi/3^N}-\frac{\sin\pi}{\pi}\right)\to\frac{3\pi}4(1-0)$ as $N\to\infty$. So the sum is $\frac{3\pi}4$ and $100\cdot\frac{3\pi}4=75\pi\approx235.6$, nearest integer $236$.

**Answer: 236**

hmmt-feb-2022-guts-29.title: Central angles must sum to $2\pi$
hmmt-feb-2022-guts-29.body:
Let $x=\frac a{a+b}\in(0,1)$, $x\ne\frac12$. A chord of length $a$ in a circle of radius $a+b$ subtends a central angle $2\arcsin\frac x2$ and a chord of length $b$ subtends $2\arcsin\frac{1-x}2$. Each angle is less than $\pi/3$, so the polygon closes up only if the central angles add up to $2\pi$:
$$f(x)=m\arcsin\frac x2+n\arcsin\frac{1-x}2=\pi.$$
$f$ is convex on $[0,1]$ ($\arcsin$ is convex on $[0,1]$), with $f(0)=\frac{n\pi}6$ and $f(1)=\frac{m\pi}6$.

- If $\max(m,n)\le6$, then $f(0),f(1)\le\pi$ and, $f$ being convex, $f<\pi$ inside $(0,1)$ (for $m=n=6$ strictly, since $f(\frac12)<\pi$); so there is no solution. We need $\max(m,n)\ge7$.
- If $\min(m,n)\le5$ (and $\max\ge7$), then $f$ is $>\pi$ at one endpoint and $<\pi$ at the other, so by the intermediate value theorem a solution exists; it is not $x=\frac12$ because $(m+n)\arcsin\frac14=\pi$ is impossible (that would need $\arcsin\frac14=\frac{\pi}{m+n}$, but $\frac\pi{\arcsin(1/4)}\approx12.43$ is not an integer).
- If $\min(m,n)\ge7$, then $f(x)\ge7\left(\arcsin\frac x2+\arcsin\frac{1-x}2\right)\ge14\arcsin\frac14>\pi$ (as $\arcsin\frac14>\frac\pi{14}$, since $\sin\frac\pi{14}<\frac\pi{14}<\frac{3.5}{14}=\frac14$), so no solution.
- If $\min(m,n)=6$ (say $n=6$, $m\ge7$): $f(0)=\pi$ and $f'(0)=\frac m2-\frac6{\sqrt3}=\frac{m-\sqrt{48}}2>0$, so $f>\pi$ on $(0,1)$ by convexity: no solution.

So the pairs with solutions are those with $\min\le5$ and $\max\ge7$. The number of pairs $(m,n)\in[1,100]^2$ with $\min\le5$ is $100^2-95^2=975$; among them those with $\max\le6$ are $6^2-1=35$ (all pairs in $[1,6]^2$ except $(6,6)$). So the count is $975-35=940$.

**Answer: 940**

hmmt-feb-2022-guts-30.title: Polar coordinates
hmmt-feb-2022-guts-30.body:
In polar coordinates $x=r\cos\theta$, $y=r\sin\theta$: $x^2+y^2=r^2$, $x^2-y^2=r^2\cos2\theta$ and $2x^3-6xy^2=2r^3\cos3\theta$. The equations become $r^{12}=r^8\cos^42\theta=8r^9\cos^33\theta$. Besides the origin, this gives $r=|\cos2\theta|$ and $r=2\cos3\theta$ (real cube roots), i.e. the intersections of the four-leaf curve $r=\cos2\theta$ with the three-leaf curve $r=2\cos3\theta$ (allowing signed $r$): $7$ points including the origin. The system is symmetric about the $x$-axis, so the $y$-contributions cancel in pairs and we only need $x$-coordinates.

All intersection points satisfy $\cos2\theta=2\cos3\theta$, i.e. with $c=\cos\theta$: $2c^2-1=2(4c^3-3c)$, i.e. $8c^3-2c^2-6c+1=0$. For a root $c=a$, $x=r\cos\theta=\cos2\theta\cos\theta=(2a^2-1)a=2a^3-a$, and each root gives two points symmetric about the $x$-axis. Therefore the required sum is $2\sum(2a^3-a)=\sum(4a^3-2a)$ over the three roots. From the cubic, $a^3=\frac{a^2}4+\frac{3a}4-\frac18$, so $4a^3-2a=a^2+a-\frac12$. By Vieta, $a+b+c=\frac14$ and $ab+bc+ca=-\frac34$, so $a^2+b^2+c^2=\frac1{16}+\frac32=\frac{25}{16}$. The sum is $\frac{25}{16}+\frac14-\frac32=\frac5{16}$, and $100a+b=500+16=516$. (A numerical computation of the six nonzero intersection points confirms the sum $0.3125$.)

**Answer: 516**

hmmt-feb-2022-guts-31.title: Complex squaring
hmmt-feb-2022-guts-31.body:
Let $\omega$ be a primitive cube root of unity and $z(P)=x+y\omega$. Then $z(f(P))=(x^2-y^2)+(2xy-y^2)\omega=x^2+2xy\omega+y^2(-1-\omega)=x^2+2xy\omega+y^2\omega^2=(x+y\omega)^2=z(P)^2$. So $z(f^n(P))=z(P)^{2^n}$, which tends to $0$ iff $|z(P)|<1$. The map $(x,y)\mapsto x+y\omega=(x-\frac y2)+\frac{\sqrt3}2y\,i$ is linear with determinant $\frac{\sqrt3}2$, so $S$ is the preimage of the unit disc and has area $\frac{\pi}{\sqrt3/2}=\frac{2\pi}{\sqrt3}=\pi\sqrt{\frac43}$. Thus $r=\frac43$ and $\lfloor100r\rfloor=133$.

**Answer: 133**

hmmt-feb-2022-guts-32.title: Sum of unit vectors
hmmt-feb-2022-guts-32.body:
With independent turns $\theta_j$ uniform on $[-\frac\pi2,\frac\pi2]$, step $k$ points in direction $\phi_k=-(\theta_2+\cdots+\theta_k)$, and $d_n^2=\left|\sum_{k=1}^ne^{i\phi_k}\right|^2=n+2\sum_{i<j}\cos(\phi_j-\phi_i)$. Now $\phi_j-\phi_i$ is minus a sum of $j-i$ independent turns, and $E[e^{i\theta}]=\frac1\pi\int_{-\pi/2}^{\pi/2}\cos\theta\,d\theta=\frac2\pi$, so $E[\cos(\phi_j-\phi_i)]=\left(\frac2\pi\right)^{j-i}$. Hence
$$a_n=n+2\sum_{t=1}^{n-1}(n-t)\left(\frac2\pi\right)^t,\qquad\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{a_n}n=1+2\sum_{t\ge1}\left(\frac2\pi\right)^t=1+\frac{4}{\pi-2}=\frac{\pi+2}{\pi-2}.$$
Numerically $\frac{\pi+2}{\pi-2}\approx4.504$, so $10\lim\frac{a_n}{n}\approx45.04$, nearest integer $45$.

**Answer: 45**

hmmt-feb-2022-guts-33.title: Estimation problem
hmmt-feb-2022-guts-33.body:
This is an estimation question about the contest data: each of the $557$ students determines exactly one subset of correctly answered problems, so $A\le557$, and many students have the same pattern (for instance several students solved no problems or only the first few easy ones), so $A$ is smaller. The official answer is $A=450$.

*Scoring:* an estimate $E$ earns $\max\bigl(0,\lfloor20-\frac23|A-E|\rfloor\bigr)$ points.

**Official answer: 450**

hmmt-feb-2022-guts-34.title: Estimation problem
hmmt-feb-2022-guts-34.body:
There are $\binom p2\approx\frac{p^2}2$ ordered triples of positive integers with sum $p$, about a quarter of which satisfy the triangle inequality ($\approx\frac{p^2}8$), and dividing by $3!$ for unordered triples gives about $\frac{p^2}{48}$ triangles of perimeter $p$; summing over $p\le n$ gives about $\frac{n^3}{144}$ triangles with perimeter at most $n$. Which $n$ to use? The largest perimeter of a degenerate-like triangle fitting in the square is about $200\sqrt2\approx283$ (a thin triangle along the diagonal), while an almost-equilateral triangle can have perimeter up to $\frac{300}{\cos15^\circ}\approx311$. A compromise $n=300$ gives $\frac{300^3}{144}=187500$, which earns $13$ points.

The exact count is $A=194162$.

*Scoring:* $\max\bigl(0,\lfloor20-|A-E|/1000\rfloor\bigr)$.

**Official answer: 194162**

hmmt-feb-2022-guts-35.title: Estimation problem
hmmt-feb-2022-guts-35.body:
Let $f(n)$ be the expected number of steps when $n$ elements are out of place. Choosing two misplaced elements $a,b$ at random, the chance that the swap puts $a$ in its correct place is $\frac1{n-1}$, and likewise for $b$; so (ignoring the small chance that both land correctly)
$$f(n)\approx1+\frac2{n-1}f(n-1)+\frac{n-3}{n-1}f(n),$$
which gives $f(n)\approx f(n-1)+\frac{n-1}2$ and hence $f(n)\approx\frac{n(n-1)}4$. A random permutation has on average $1$ fixed point, so about $99$ elements are misplaced, and $f(99)\approx\frac{99\cdot98}4\approx2425$, which earns $19$ points.

The exact value is $A=2427$.

*Scoring:* $\max\bigl(0,\lfloor20-\frac12|A-E|\rfloor\bigr)$.

**Official answer: 2427**

hmmt-feb-2022-guts-36.title: Estimation problem
hmmt-feb-2022-guts-36.body:
Fix $a,b$. The derivative $P'(x)=3x^2+2ax+b$ has a root near $r\approx-\frac b{2a}$, small compared with $100$, and $P(r)\approx-\frac{b^2}{4a}$; the value of $c$ giving the closest pair of roots is the integer nearest to $-P(r)$. Writing $-P(r)=c+s$ with $s$ roughly uniform on $(-\frac12,\frac12)$, the two close roots differ by about $2\sqrt{|s|/a}$ and the third root is near $-a$, so $M(P)\approx\frac12\sqrt{a^3/|s|}$. Large $M$ needs $a$ large.

For a threshold $L$ we need $|s|<\frac{a^3}{(2L)^2}$; summing over $a,b\le100$ the expected number of polynomials with $M>L$ is about $\frac{2\cdot100\cdot100^4/4}{(2L)^2}$. Setting this to $20$ gives $L^2=\frac{10^{10}}{160}$, $L\approx7900$, which earns $14$ points.

The exact value is $A=8097$.

*Scoring:* $\max\bigl(0,\lfloor20-20|3\ln(A/E)|^{1/2}\rfloor\bigr)$.

**Official answer: 8097**
